summary: Root cause identified with high confidence (0.78): the portfolio-service v4.5.0 deploy dep-5905 at 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z introduced a new unindexed trades query ('SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at') that runs a 48.2M-row Seq Scan against the shared ledger-db, driving ledger-db CPU to ~95-97% and active connections to ~190 and starving order-service's INSERT INTO orders past statement_timeout (p99 ~5s). The change point is coincident with the deploy, not with the DBA autovacuum change cfg-2903 at 08:00:00Z, and the repeated slow query matches the deploy's declared change verbatim with application_name=portfolio-service. The reporter's autovacuum suspicion (H2) and the infrastructure/co-tenant hypotheses (H3/H4) are rejected on timing, mechanism (no lock/deadlock/IO-wait/vacuum-worker log entries in the full 392-entry ledger-db set), flat disk, and no pooler in topology. Residual uncertainty (hence the 0.78 cap rather than higher): sub-2-minute ordering between the 08:56 deploy and the 08:55-labelled metric bucket is unresolvable at 120s resolution, and H1's scope claim that shared-ledger-db saturation starves ALL direct consumers is partly contradicted by payment-service and settlement-service showing no degradation.

ranked_hypotheses.title: portfolio-service v4.5.0 new unindexed trades query saturates shared ledger-db (bad deploy)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The dep-5905 deploy of portfolio-service v4.5.0 at 08:56:00Z introduced a new query 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at' that performs a 48.2M-row Seq Scan on the shared ledger-db. ledger-db is consumed directly by four services (order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service, settlement-service); the scan drives ledger-db CPU to ~95-97% and active connections to ~190, starving order-service's INSERT INTO orders past statement_timeout and driving its p99 to ~5s. portfolio-service degrades hardest (p99 ~7s) as it is both the scan's source and a victim. The 08:55-labelled 'onset' reported earlier is a bucket-alignment artifact: at 2-minute resolution the last healthy point is the 08:55 bucket and the first degraded point is 08:57, placing the change point at the deploy instant and inside the same window as the deploy.

causal_chain.claim: dep-5905 deploys portfolio-service v4.5.0 at 08:56:00Z introducing 'new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at', with no migration.
portfolio-service holds a DIRECT db edge to ledger-db (confirmed from topology), so its new query executes directly against the shared instance.
The deployed query executes against ledger-db as a large Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907), application_name=portfolio-service — matching the deploy's declared change verbatim in structure.
The scan drives ledger-db slow_queries_per_min from ~1/min to 70-146/min and CPU from ~30% to ~95-97% and active connections from 62 to ~190.

The change point of ledger-db CPU/connections/slow-queries is the 08:55-08:57 window (last flat at the 08:55 bucket, first degraded at 08:57), coincident with the 08:56 deploy; the first slow query is 08:58:38Z, 2.6 min after the deploy.
Shared ledger-db saturation starves order-service; its INSERT INTO orders exceed statement_timeout (first 09:00:42Z), driving p99 to ~5s.
portfolio-service degrades even harder than order-service (p99 ~7s) as both source and victim.

assumptions: The new query lacks an index supporting (account_id, executed_at), producing the Seq Scan; inferred from F9/F32's Seq Scan plan (no migration shipped, F2).
ledger-db has no per-service connection cap and no pooler (F20/F4 confirm no pooler node), so portfolio-service's scan load can saturate the instance and starve order-service.
The ~2.6-minute lag between deploy and first slow query at 08:58:38 reflects connection/execution ramp, not a different cause.

payment-service/settlement-service did not degrade (F33) because their tiny result sets/tables are still served from cache/buffers while CPU is consumed by the trades scan — a load-proportional effect, not a counter-example.

ranked_hypotheses.title: ledger-db host resource/IOPS starvation by co-tenant workload (resource exhaustion / infrastructure)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: ledger-db sits on a shared cloud volume/host and is starved of IOPS or CPU by another tenant workload, causing transaction timeouts for all db consumers. This mirrors historical precedent HIST-110 (volume burst credits exhausted, IOPS throttled) rather than any tracked config or deploy.

causal_chain.claim: ledger-db runs on a shared host/volume subject to burst-credit or tenant contention.
A co-tenant workload or burst-credit exhaustion throttles IOPS, starving ledger-db at 08:56.
Starved ledger-db slows order-service INSERTs to statement timeout.

assumptions: Some external workload started at exactly 08:56Z with no tracked deploy or config change and with a query signature coincidentally appearing as application_name=portfolio-service.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Speculative and now contradicted by mechanism: the CPU/connection rise is attributed to a specific, named, deployed query (48.2M-row Seq Scan with application_name=portfolio-service) that matches dep-5905's declared change verbatim (F9,F14,F32); no IOPS/host-level contention signal is present; disk is flat (F12); and no untracked co-tenant event is observable in any finding. The HIST-110 precedent is a weak, category-level analogy.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Infrastructure-level host/network sharing or hidden pooler beneath ledger-db that is not modelled as a topology node
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The change point at ledger-db originates below the reachable topology: a shared host, network path, or un-modelled proxy/pooler degrades at 08:56 and starves ledger-db independently of any tracked deploy, with the dep-5905 query merely co-occurring. Evidence: the dependency graph is known not to model host co-tenancy or reverse-proxy/network-layer sharing.

causal_chain.claim: Ledger-db's host or a network/proxy layer not represented as a graph node degrades or contends at ~08:56.
The degradation throttles ledger-db IO/CPU, producing the Seq Scan timeouts and order-service statement timeouts.

assumptions: A host/network fault began at exactly 08:56Z, coincident with but unrelated to the only deploy in the window, and coincidentally the repeated slow query is the exact query introduced by that deploy.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Resting on an unobservable layer while the observable mechanism (the portfolio-service Seq Scan matching dep-5905 verbatim) fully explains the symptom; no host/network metric shows an independent change point; the build runs on a flagged assumption that requires two coincidences. Retained only as the claimed residual gap.

ranked_hypotheses.title: DBA autovacuum scale-factor change on ledger-db causes bloat/lock-driven statement timeouts (reporter's suspicion)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: cfg-2903 reduced autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor from 0.2 to 0.1 on ledger-db at 08:00:00Z. More aggressive autovacuum triggers vacuum workers that consume IO/CPU and hold locks on trades, delaying queries and causing statement timeouts in order-service. Evidence: the config change is real, it is the only config change in the window, and it precedes the incident.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-2903 lowers autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.1 on ledger-db at 08:00:00Z.
More aggressive autovacuum causes vacuum workers to run on the large trades table.
Vacuum work consumes IO/CPU and takes locks, slowing concurrent queries.
Slow/locked queries on ledger-db cause statement timeouts in order-service and slow portfolio-service queries.

assumptions: Autovacuum fired on trades shortly after 08:00 and held locks (never observed).
The 56-minute quiet gap could be autovacuum's delayed trigger rather than evidence against the hypothesis (now also contradicted by the 08:58:38 onset).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Fully contradicted: (a) timing — cfg-2903 landed 08:00:00Z, and at 2-minute resolution ledger-db CPU/connections/slow_queries are flat through the 08:55 bucket and only break at 08:57, i.e. ~56 min later and coincident with the 08:56 deploy, not with the config change (F29,F30,F31,F32); (b) mechanism — the entire ledger-db log set (392 entries, truncated=false) contains only four patterns, none of which is an autovacuum-worker, Vacuum/Rewrite, lock-wait or IO-wait message; targeted contains='lock'/'deadlock'/'IO'/'Rewr' queries all return 0 (F23,F24,F25,F26,F27); (c) the only recurring autovacuum activity is 13 'processed table public.audit_log' lines running steadily 08:08-10:55 with no burst and no lock/vacuum trace on trades (F24,F28); (d) disk usage is flat, ruling out bloat/disk-driven slowness (F12); (e) no prior precedent ties an autovacuum scale-factor reduction to this symptom (F17).

facts.statement: Exactly one deploy landed in 08:00-11:00Z across all services: dep-5905, portfolio-service v4.5.0 at 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z (author k.shah), status 'live', rolled_back_at null, declaring 'new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at' and 'no migration included'. No order-service deploy exists in the window.
Exactly one config change landed in the window: cfg-2903 on ledger-db, autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1, at 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z by dba-team.
ledger-db is a shared postgres instance (owner platform, shared=true) with direct db edges from exactly four services: order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service.

portfolio-service holds a direct db edge to ledger-db in its topology graph (portfolio-service->ledger-db kind 'db'), so the coupling is confirmed from topology, not just from the application_name string.
No connection pooler or shared host node exists in front of ledger-db in any of the four consumer graphs; ledger-db is reached by direct db edges in all four.

At 2-minute resolution ledger-db is flat through the 08:55:00Z bucket (cpu 29.62 avg / max 30.33; connections_active 62.31) and only breaks at 08:57:00Z (cpu 63.88 avg / max 95.62; connections 122.61), reaching ~94-97% CPU and ~178-199 connections thereafter; the '08:55' onset is a bucket-alignment artifact.
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min was ~0.59-1.29/min through the 08:55 bucket (avg 1.29) and jumped 54x to 70.25 (max 139.17) at 08:57:00Z, holding ~135-146/min.

The first ledger-db slow query is at 08:58:38Z (8690ms) and is the single repeated signature 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at -- Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907) application_name=portfolio-service'; all 360 WARN entries in the window are this one signature.
order-service degraded in the same window: p99 was flat ~148-156ms from 07:00 to 08:50, then jumped (08:55 bucket avg 1240.72ms, max 5607.8) and held ~5000-5400ms through 10:55.
order-service's only significant error is downstream of the DB: 284 ERROR entries 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)', first seen 09:00:42Z.

portfolio-service — the application_name on every slow ledger-db query — degraded in the same window and harder than order-service: p99 flat 178-187ms through the 08:55 point, then 3523.96ms at 08:57 and ~6700-7340ms thereafter.

The full 08:00-11:00Z ledger-db log set is 392 entries (truncated=false) reducing to exactly four patterns: 360 trades Seq Scan WARNs, 18 'checkpoint complete' INFO, 13 'autovacuum: processed table public.audit_log' INFO, and 1 cfg-2903 applied INFO.

No lock-wait, deadlock, IO-wait, Vacuum/Rewrite or autovacuum-worker message exists anywhere in the ledger-db window; targeted contains='lock', 'deadlock', 'IO' (WARN) and 'Rewr' queries all returned total_matched=0 with truncated=false.

The only recurring autovacuum activity is 13 'processed table public.audit_log' lines running steadily 08:08:06Z-10:55:51Z with no burst, no table other than audit_log, and no tie to trades or the slow queries; cfg-2903 produced exactly one log line at 08:00:20Z.

Historical precedent HIST-111 (2025-05-22) 'Reporting job full table scans slowed ledger-db' has the same mechanism (new query without index doing sequential scans, category bad_deployment); a search for 'autovacuum settings change database slowness' returned count 0.
payment-service and settlement-service (two direct ledger-db consumers) show no degradation across the window: p99 flat ~287-354ms and ~213-272ms respectively, with no step at 08:55/08:56.

assumptions: The new trades query lacks an index supporting (account_id, executed_at), producing the observed Seq Scan; this is inferred from the Seq Scan plan on 48.2M rows and 'no migration included' in the deploy (F9/F32/F2), not directly verified via schema inspection or EXPLAIN.
ledger-db has no per-service connection cap and no pooler (F20/F4 confirm no pooler node), so portfolio-service's scan load can saturate the instance and starve order-service.
The ~2.6-minute lag between the deploy (08:56:00Z) and the first slow query (08:58:38Z) reflects connection/execution ramp, not a different cause.

payment-service and settlement-service did not degrade (F33) because their small result sets/tables are still served from cache/buffers while CPU is consumed by the trades scan — a load-proportional effect, not a counter-example to ledger-db saturation.
The '08:55' first-degraded bucket reflects sampling alignment; the true change point lies in the 08:55:00-08:56:59 window coincident with the 08:56:00Z deploy.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The deploy's declared change matches the dominant ledger-db slow-query signature verbatim in structure, so the deployed artifact and the query causing the scan are the same component.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The deploy landed 08:56:00Z, ~2.6 min before the first slow query (08:58:38) and ~4.7 min before order-service's first statement timeout (09:00:42), whereas cfg-2903 landed ~56 min before the first slow query.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) ledger-db disk usage is flat across the whole incident (69.36-72.5%, mean 71.01) with no trend change at onset, arguing against disk exhaustion or bloat.

timeline.event: DBA config change cfg-2903 applied on ledger-db: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 (single log line at 08:00:20Z); ledger-db remains flat on all metrics.
Steady, low-volume autovacuum activity begins on public.audit_log only (13 lines through 10:55:51Z, no burst, no trades involvement).
Last fully healthy samples: order-service p99 ~148-156ms, portfolio-service p99 ~187ms, ledger-db CPU 29.62 avg, connections 62.31, slow_queries ~1.29/min, disk ~71.8%.
portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployed (dep-5905, k.shah), introducing the new unindexed trades query filtered by account_id + executed_at; remains 'live'.

First degraded 2-minute bucket: ledger-db CPU 63.88 avg (max 95.62), connections_active 122.61 (max 185.11), slow_queries_per_min 70.25 (54x jump); portfolio-service p99 3523.96ms; the 08:55-labelled bucket was still flat.
First ledger-db slow query logged: 8690ms Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907) with application_name=portfolio-service — the signature that repeats 360 times.
First order-service statement timeout: 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)'; 284 such errors follow.
Incident INC-009 reported by on-call SRE: order-service p99 > 5s with ledger-db statement timeouts.
Degradation persists: order-service p99 ~5000-5400ms, portfolio-service p99 ~6700-7340ms, ledger-db CPU ~94-97%, connections ~190, slow queries ~135-146/min.
Last observed occurrence of the portfolio-service trades Seq Scan WARN in the captured window.

recommended_actions.action: Roll back dep-5905 (portfolio-service v4.5.0) to the prior release immediately; this removes the unindexed trades query from ledger-db.
recommended_actions.rationale: dep-5905 is the only deploy in the window, is still 'live' with rolled_back_at null, and its declared change matches verbatim the 48.2M-row Seq Scan (application_name=portfolio-service) that drives ledger-db CPU to ~95-97% and connections to ~190, starving order-service INSERTs (F2, F14, F9, F5, F29, F30, F31).

recommended_actions.action: After rollback, verify recovery on the same signals that moved: ledger-db cpu_pct back toward ~30%, connections_active back toward ~62, slow_queries_per_min back to ~1/min, and order-service p99 back toward ~150ms within 10-15 minutes.
recommended_actions.rationale: The bulk of false-positive risk in H1 is the sub-2-minute ordering between the 08:56 deploy and the 08:55-08:57 metric bucket (F16, F34); a clean recovery on rollback is the strongest available confirmation of causality.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back or revert cfg-2903 (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1) on this evidence: it landed 56 minutes before onset, produced a single log line, and no autovacuum/lock/IO-wait mechanism ties it to the incident.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2 is fully contradicted: 56-minute gap, no autovacuum-worker/Vacuum/lock/deadlock/IO-wait entries in the full 392-entry set, flat disk, and zero precedent for autovacuum scale-factor changes causing this symptom (F1, F17, F23, F24, F25, F26, F12, F6).

recommended_actions.action: Add a composite index on trades (account_id, executed_at) via a proper migration, and gate the v4.5.0 release on a reviewed EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) showing an index scan instead of a 48.2M-row Seq Scan, before re-deploying the new query.
recommended_actions.rationale: The observed plan is a Seq Scan on 48.2M rows and the deploy shipped 'no migration included'; this is the same mechanism as precedent HIST-111 (new unindexed query doing sequential scans) (F9, F32, F2, F14, F6).

recommended_actions.action: Instrument and enforce protection on the shared ledger-db: per-service connection limits (or a pooler) plus a statement/query-cost guard, so one consumer's scan cannot drive instance-wide CPU to ~95% and starve the others.
recommended_actions.rationale: ledger-db is shared by four direct consumers with no pooler or per-service cap in topology, which is what allowed portfolio-service's scan to propagate to order-service (F3, F20, F22, F18).

recommended_actions.action: Reconcile the apparent scope discrepancy: capture per-consumer ledger-db load and, at finer than 4-minute resolution, confirm why payment-service and settlement-service were unaffected while order-service and portfolio-service were not.
recommended_actions.rationale: F33 shows two of the four direct ledger-db clients, payment-service (~287-354ms) and settlement-service (~213-272ms), never degraded; H1's scope claim that shared-ledger-db saturation starves ALL direct consumers rests on an unverified load-proportional/caching assumption (F33, F22).

recommended_actions.action: Add a pre-merge/pre-deploy gate that flags new queries on shared datastores without a supporting index or a reviewed EXPLAIN, and add per-service connection/CPU saturation alerting on ledger-db with a p99 and slow-query SLO.
recommended_actions.rationale: The pre-deploy review missed a query whose plan performs a full scan of a 48.2M-row table, and no alert fired before the 09:10Z report even though ledger-db CPU/connections broke at 08:57 (F2, F9, F23, F29, F30, F31, F6).

recommended_actions.action: Update runbooks so a ledger-db-statement-timeout incident first checks recent deploys on ALL direct ledger-db consumers (order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service, settlement-service), not just the reporting service, and de-prioritises same-window config changes lacking a mechanism.
recommended_actions.rationale: The initial suspicion was the DBA autovacuum change (H2), while the actual change point aligned with a deploy on a different service sharing ledger-db (F1, F2, F3, F13, F29, F31).

data_gaps: Sub-2-minute ordering between the 08:56:00Z deploy and the 08:55:00-08:56:59 metric bucket is unresolvable: ledger-db metric buckets are 120s wide and no finer series was available, so the deploy cannot be strictly proven to precede the change point (F16, F34).

No schema or EXPLAIN evidence was obtained for the trades table: the absence of an index on (account_id, executed_at) is inferred from the observed Seq Scan plan and 'no migration included', not directly verified.

No per-edge pooler/host/proxy attribute exists in the dependency graph, so host-level co-tenancy or a network-layer/reverse-proxy path outside the modelled topology cannot be observed or fully excluded (F20 rules out only graph-modelled poolers).

No metric series exposing autovacuum worker counts, bloat or vacuum timestamps was retrieved; cfg-2903's autovacuum trigger behaviour at 08:00 onward is inferred from log text and the absence of any vacuum message, not directly measured.

The full per-line enumeration of all 360 WARN entries was not visually confirmed (WARN entry view was truncated at 40 rows); the zero-count conclusion for lock/deadlock/IO/Rewrite/vacuum-worker terms rests on per-term count queries with truncated=false plus the top_patterns count=360 aggregate.

payment-service and settlement-service p99 buckets are 240s wide, so a brief sub-4-minute spike coincident with 08:56 could be smoothed away; their 'no degradation' state is robust only at the 4-minute level.
Blast radius beyond order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service (other ledger-db clients or downstream callers) was not measured.
No deploy-to-first-request correlation data was available to bound the ramp from deploy to first heavy scan.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Rollback of dep-5905 (or removal of the trades query from ledger-db) fails to restore ledger-db CPU/connections, slow_queries_per_min and order-service p99 to baseline — this would falsify H1 and shift attention to a cause on ledger-db itself (H3/H4).

A ledger-db signal (CPU, connections, slow queries) is shown to rise strictly before 08:56:00Z at finer than 120s resolution, with the Seq Scan starting only afterwards — this would break the deploy-coincidence argument and reopen timing-based hypotheses (including cfg-2903).

Discovery of an index on trades(account_id, executed_at) that the query does not use, or evidence of an unmodelled pooler/host bottleneck, would weaken the 'unindexed query saturates shared ledger-db' mechanism.

Observation of lock-wait, deadlock, IO-wait, Vacuum/Rewrite or autovacuum-worker entries on ledger-db in the incident window (from a full, untruncated log enumeration) would restore a mechanism for H2 or a contention-based hypothesis.

Evidence that payment-service and settlement-service were in fact degraded at sub-4-minute resolution — or that they consume ledger-db via a different/smaller path — would resolve the scope discrepancy in F33 and either strengthen or partly falsify H1's blast-radius claim.
A second, independent workload or event on ledger-db at ~08:56 that is not attributable to portfolio-service would reintroduce H3/H4.

findings.statement: ledger-db is a shared postgres instance (owner platform, shared=true, has_telemetry=true) with direct db edges from four services: order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service; api-gateway calls order-service, portfolio-service and payment-service over http. So the blast radius of anything on ledger-db includes all four db consumers, not just order-service.

order-service's own dependency graph shows no connection pooler, shared host or shared cache in front of ledger-db: its edges are order-service->ledger-db (db), ->pricing-engine (http), ->exchange-gateway (http), ->kafka (queue-produce), plus api-gateway->order-service. The shared infrastructure it touches beyond ledger-db is kafka and redis-cache (both reached via pricing-engine), so no pooler/DB-instance-level sharing with portfolio-service was observed in the returned topology.

The deployment on the ledger-db-adjacent service (portfolio-service v4.5.0, dep-5905) landed at 08:56:00Z, i.e. ~56 minutes AFTER the autovacuum config change at 08:00:00Z and ~14 minutes before the 09:10Z incident report; it introduces a new trades query with no migration and is still 'live' (not rolled back).

Historical precedent search for 'ledger-db statement timeouts' returned two incidents with the same symptom signature but different root causes: HIST-110 (2026-01-15) 'Slow orders from ledger-db IOPS throttling' - root cause 'Cloud volume burst credits exhausted; IOPS throttled'; HIST-111 (2025-05-22) 'Reporting job full table scans slowed ledger-db' - root cause 'New report query without index did sequential scans' (category bad_deployment). A second search for 'autovacuum settings change database slowness' returned count 0, so there is no prior autovacuum-related precedent.

Its logs show 239 WARN 'holdings P&L query took <n>ms for account <n>' entries from 08:59:39 (e.g. 7459ms for account 38649). Blast radius therefore includes at least portfolio-service as a co-victim/co-culprit, not just order-service.

ledger-db disk is flat across the whole incident, arguing against disk exhaustion: disk_used_pct ranges only 69.36-72.5 (mean 71.01, first 71.11, last 70.89) with no trend change at 08:55 (71.81 avg at 08:50 → 71.15 at 08:55 → 70.66 at 09:00). The 08:55 step change is confined to CPU/connections, and the repeated error is a large Seq Scan (48.2M rows), which is consistent with scan/CPU + connection-pressure starvation rather than a disk-full or (on the evidence seen) a lock-contention signature.

Re-query of the full 06:00-11:00Z window across ALL services confirms exactly one deploy (dep-5905, portfolio-service v4.5.0, 08:56:00Z, author k.shah, status live, rolled_back_at null) and exactly one config change (cfg-2903, ledger-db autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1, 08:00:00Z, dba-team). No order-service deploy and no pooler/schema/connection-limit change appears in the window.

The deploy's declared change matches the dominant ledger-db slow-query signature verbatim in structure: deploy change 'new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at' vs the repeated DB WARN 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2' with 'application_name=portfolio-service'. The deployed artifact and the query causing the scan are the same component.

findings.statement: Timing comparison: the deploy landed 08:56:00Z, i.e. ~2 minutes before ledger-db's first slow query (08:58:38) and ~4.7 minutes before order-service's first statement timeout (09:00:42); the config change landed 08:00:00Z, i.e. ~56 min before the first slow query and ~55 min before the earliest metric degradation bucket (08:55). Only the deploy is temporally adjacent to onset.

Caveat on the timing alignment: the deploy at 08:56 falls ~1-3 minutes AFTER the first bucket in which the metrics already show degradation (onset bucket 08:55, order-service p99 1240.72ms, ledger-db cpu 56.67 avg), so the deploy does not strictly precede the change point; a cause that actually started within the 08:55 bucket cannot be excluded on timing alone. The strongest identification of the deploy is the exact query/application_name match, not the timestamps.

findings.statement: portfolio-service has a DIRECT db edge to ledger-db: the downstream graph (depth 1 and depth 2, partial=false) lists edges portfolio-service->ledger-db kind 'db', portfolio-service->market-data-service 'http', portfolio-service->redis-cache 'cache'; ledger-db is a postgres node owner platform, shared=true. H1's portfolio-service->ledger-db coupling is therefore confirmed from topology, not just the application_name string.

No connection pooler or shared host node exists anywhere in the returned topology for portfolio-service, order-service, payment-service or settlement-service: ledger-db is reached by direct db edges in all four graphs (e.g. payment-service edges are only ledger-db db, bank-partner-api external, kafka queue-produce; settlement-service only kafka queue-consume and ledger-db db). The shared-pooler variant of H3 is ruled out — there is no pooler intermediary in front of ledger-db.

The only shared cache visible in these graphs is redis-cache (redis, owner platform, shared=true). portfolio-service reaches it directly (portfolio-service->redis-cache kind 'cache') and indirectly via market-data-service; order-service has no redis-cache edge in its own graph (its redis-cache touch was noted as reached via pricing-engine). So portfolio-service and order-service do not share a cache edge directly.

Shared-component overlap between portfolio-service and order-service in topology is limited to ledger-db (both hold a direct db edge to it, and it is shared=true); portfolio-service's other outbound targets (market-data-service, redis-cache) are not outbound targets of order-service. payment-service and settlement-service also hold direct ledger-db db edges, so ledger-db is the single common dependency of the four db consumers.

findings.statement: ledger-db cpu_pct at 2-minute resolution is FLAT through the bucket labelled 08:55:00Z (avg 29.62, max 30.33) and only jumps in the next bucket 08:57:00Z (avg 63.88, max 95.62), then 95.22 at 08:59 and ~94-97% thereafter. This places the CPU change-point inside the 08:55-08:57 window, i.e. coincident with the 08:56 deploy, not earlier.

ledger-db connections_active steps in the identical bucket: flat 62.31 (max 64.78) at the 08:55:00Z point, then 122.61 (max 185.11) at 08:57:00Z, 195.84 (max 199.81) at 08:59:00Z, holding ~178-193. CPU and connections share one change point, so the '08:55' onset previously reported is a bucket-alignment artifact — the last healthy point is the 08:55 bucket and the first degraded point is 08:57.

ledger-db slow_queries_per_min confirms the same change point and is the strongest single signal: ~0.59-1.29/min for all buckets up to and including 08:55:00Z (avg 1.29), then a 54x jump to 70.25 (max 139.17) at 08:57:00Z and 144.25 (max 148.81) at 08:59:00Z, holding ~135-146/min. Slow queries were therefore ~zero/min at 08:55 and only began at scale after 08:56.

findings.statement: payment-service (a direct ledger-db consumer) shows NO degradation: latency_p99_ms is flat 287.66-353.78ms (mean 317.94) for the whole 08:30-10:00Z window — 327.87 at 08:50, 315.85 at 08:54, 312.48 at 08:58, 313.48 at 09:02, and ~307-328 thereafter. There is no step at ~08:55/08:56. Same for settlement-service: flat 213.5-271.99ms (mean 239.82), 239.42 at 08:50, 246.69 at 08:54, 242.2 at 08:58, 249.28 at 09:02. The shared-ledger-db saturation therefore did NOT propagate to these two consumers.

portfolio-service p99 at 2-minute resolution shows the SAME alignment: flat 178.01-187.14ms through the 08:55:00Z point (avg 187.14, max 192.6), then 3523.96 (max 6870.64) at 08:57:00Z and 6923.18 (max 7056.7) at 08:59:00Z, holding ~6700-7340ms. So portfolio-service's app-level p99 and ledger-db's own CPU/connections/slow-queries all break in the 08:55-08:57 window, i.e. at the deploy instant 08:56:00Z, not before it. This is consistent with the deploy being the trigger and argues against a pre-existing 08:55 cause (autovacuum, config change at 08:00) — but note app p99 and DB metrics are sampled at the same 120s grid, so within-bucket ordering between the 08:56 deploy and the 08:55-08:57 bucket contents cannot be strictly established from metrics alone.
